Fracture Lines: Dominion · strategy guide

The principles and the important steps that keep you competitive. There's no single right way to win, so this guide points the way and leaves the details to you.

Know how the game is won

A standard game ends after 200 turns. Before then, a power can win by finishing the Corridor Engine, or by conquest, being the last one standing. If neither happens, the highest score wins. The computer players are racing for these too.

Keep an eye on the Objectives tab. It shows where you stand in each race, and its Threats list tells you when a rival is getting close. Being competitive means knowing, at every stage, which race you're in and who you have to beat.

Principles

  • Growth compounds. Every world you settle early keeps paying for the rest of the game. Early expansion is rarely wasted.
  • Have a goal, and keep a backup. Pick the victory that suits your position, but keep your score healthy in case it slips away.
  • Balance your empire. Industry, science, credits and defense all matter. An empire strong in one and starved in the others is easy to beat.
  • Information wins. Explore constantly, and watch your rivals' progress. Most defeats come as a surprise.
  • Act on threats early. A rival's plan is far easier to stop when it begins than when it's nearly done.
  • Don't waste what you have. Idle yards, idle fleets, a growing debt or an unused Focus are all lost turns.
  • Adapt. Your plan should follow the galaxy you're dealt: where the good worlds are, who your neighbours are, and what they're doing.

The early game

  • Explore first. Find the good worlds, the ruins and anomalies, and your neighbours as soon as you can.
  • Settle steadily. Keep claiming worlds and outposts while there's open space near you. Territory taken early is cheap; taken later, it means a war.
  • Lay the foundations. Early research and buildings that raise industry, science and credits on every world make everything after them faster.
  • Keep some defense. You don't need a big fleet yet, but you do need enough to answer raiders and opportunists.
  • Make contact. Meeting your neighbours early opens trade and tells you who may become a threat.

The middle game

  • Develop your best worlds. Your largest worlds are your engines: build them up before spreading effort thin.
  • Connect your economy. Trade between your worlds and with friendly powers adds up, and so do outposts that sell fuel and exotics.
  • Commit to a direction. By now you should know which victory you're aiming for, and research and build toward it.
  • Keep your fleet current. New research reaches ships already in service only when they're refitted. A modern fleet beats a larger outdated one.
  • Secure your borders. Fortify the worlds that face your rivals, and keep a fleet where trouble is likeliest.
  • Watch the leader. If someone is pulling ahead, decide whether you can out-race them or must slow them down.

The late game

  • Close out. Whatever your path, the end is a race: concentrate everything on finishing first.
  • Stop the others. If a rival is close to winning, nothing you build matters more than stopping them.
  • Prepare for the crisis. If the Wardens are coming, have defenses and a strong fleet ready before they wake.
  • Protect what wins you the game. Your capital, and whatever you've built or found there, are what rivals will come for.

Choosing a path to victory

The Corridor Engine

A long research path, then a great work at your capital. It rewards a strong science economy, a well-developed capital and steady defense while you build. It's the path the computer players favour, so it's also the race you're most likely to have to win, or to stop.

Conquest

Taking worlds from others. It rewards a strong economy behind a modern fleet, careful preparation, and patience: a world's defenses must be overcome and its orbit held before it can be taken. Supply, fuel and refits decide how far you can reach. Each world you take adds to you and weakens a rival.

Score

The fallback that's always in play. Score grows with your worlds and their people, your research, your fleet, and the treasures and victories you collect. A balanced, wide empire scores well, whatever else it's doing.

Open games

In an open game the Engine is a prize to hold rather than a victory. Holding it brings great advantages, and the resentment of everyone else. Be ready to defend it, or to take it.

Playing to your people's strengths

The Concord

Restless energy: Colony and outpost ships cost 25% less, and new colonies start with 2 population.

Settling is cheap for you and new colonies start strong. Your strength is growth: the wider you spread early, the more everything else pays off later.

The Tessan Dynasties

Old money: +25% credits from every world, and trade treaties pay double.

Credits are your strength, and trade multiplies them. Friends are worth more to you than to anyone, and money can buy what others must build.

The Kel Hives

Hive-cities: Worlds hold 2 more population, and population grows faster.

Your worlds hold more people and grow faster. Big, well-developed worlds are your strength, and a large population serves every path to victory.

The Hegemony Remnant

Imperial legions: Warships hit on +1, and troop transports land twice the force.

Your warships hit harder and your troops land in greater force. War is your strength: every world you take is one your rivals no longer have.

The Vael Living Fleets

Living hulls: Ships move 1 hex farther and repair a point of hull every turn, anywhere.

Your living ships go farther, heal anywhere and need no fuel. Reach is your strength: you can act where others can't follow.

The Mirrun Commonwealth

Pelagic scholars: +20% science on every world, and Ocean worlds hold 3 more population.

Science is your strength, and ocean worlds are your home. Settle the seas, out-research your rivals, and let your knowledge do the fighting.

The Ylith Aeries

Far sight: Ships and worlds see 2 hexes farther, and scouts and colony ships move 1 faster.

You see farther and spread faster than anyone. Information and early expansion are your strengths: find the best worlds first, and never be surprised.

The Zhaq Free Republics

Never again: Their worlds' garrisons are half again as strong and never weaken under siege, and a besieged world starves half as fast.

Your worlds are very hard to take. Defense is your strength: hold what you claim, let attackers break on your walls, and strike when they're spent.

Any people can win any way. Your trait just makes some paths easier, so lean into it when you can.

War

  • Fight on your terms. Choose when and where. Attacking prepared defenses with too little is the fastest way to lose a fleet.
  • Concentrate. Strength in one place beats the same strength spread thin.
  • Quality matters. Better technology and refitted ships often matter more than numbers.
  • Mind your supply. Fleets far from home run short. Plan how you'll keep them fuelled before you go.
  • Finish what you start. Taking a world means winning its orbit, holding it, and bringing enough troops. Leave halfway and you'll start again.
  • Once you're in a battle, you're committed. A fleet that shares a hex with the enemy can't just sail off. Pulling back is an order of its own, and it costs a last exchange of fire. Decide before you engage whether you can win.
  • Withdraw while you still have a fleet. A beaten fleet that survives can be repaired, refitted and sent back. One that fights to the last can't.
  • Use your fleet in pieces when it pays. Detaching part of a fleet lets you screen a world, chase a weaker enemy or pull damaged ships out, without giving up your main force.
  • Respect orbital guns. Dug-in batteries fire first and finish off damaged ships. Bring enough to silence them quickly, or they'll grind a fleet down. Once they're out, they stay out while you hold the orbit.
  • Know when to make peace. A war that costs more than it gains is worth ending.

Fuel and supply

  • Fuel is a budget. Your empire keeps a reserve. Moving, refuelling and pushing ships harder all draw on it, and running short slows everything down.
  • Depots are what keep you moving. They make most of the fuel and let you store more. An empire with few depots can't keep many fleets in motion for long.
  • Stock up in peacetime. A full reserve is what lets you fight a long war, or answer a surprise.
  • Tankers carry your reach. Fuel tankers travelling with a fleet keep it going beyond supply, and parked ones extend your lines. Plan any deep strike around them.
  • Burn hard when speed decides it. Arriving a turn sooner can save a world or win a race, but it costs fuel you may want later.
  • Your rivals have the same limits. Raiding their depots, or catching them far from supply, can stop a war before it reaches you.

Defense

  • Defend where it matters. Your capital, your best worlds and your borders come first.
  • Fixed defenses buy time. Guns in orbit hold off small attacks and give your fleets time to arrive.
  • Respond quickly. A world under siege loses output every turn. Break sieges early.
  • Batteries punish small attacks. Orbital guns make raids and probing attacks costly. Pair them with a fleet that can arrive before a big attack silences them.
  • Don't leave your heart empty. A rival who finds your capital unguarded can undo a whole game.

Threats from outside

  • Pirates and creatures belong to no one and trouble everyone. Deal with them when you're ready. They pay well when destroyed. Sometimes buying peace from pirates is the better use of your time. Neighbours can help each other against them.
  • The Wardens are the late-game crisis, and they come for every power, the strongest and anyone building the Corridor Engine first. The signs come long before they wake: deal with what you can while it's still asleep. Awake, they spread like an empire, and they come back unless every trace of them is gone.
  • Adjust the challenge to your taste: the number of pirates and creatures, the difficulty and the computer players' options are all settings.

Exploration

  • Keep exploring all game. Ruins and anomalies give research, and some hide relics of the old empires.
  • Treat fuel as a budget. Depots are what let you keep fleets moving through a long war. Build up the reserve in peacetime, and save burning hard for when speed decides the outcome.
  • Keep a scout or two all game. When a corridor collapses, whoever charts the new route first gets research, and the route back.
  • Plan for new sectors. In a long game the map grows, and you hear what kind of sector is coming before it opens. Have scouts and settlers ready, and be ready to defend what you claim: a new sector is a fresh race.
  • Relics are powerful, and they stay with the world that keeps them. Guard yours; a rival's can be taken.
  • The galaxy may be bigger than it looks. Be ready to move if new space opens.
  • Some space is sealed. Getting into a sealed sector takes the right technology, or a beacon that opens it for everyone. Being first in is worth a lot; opening it for your rivals is a choice to make on purpose.
  • The network can change. Corridors rarely collapse, but when one does it can cut an empire in two. Don't depend on a single route to your most important worlds.

Diplomacy

  • Friends are an economy. Trade and good relations pay steadily and keep wars away from you.
  • Choose your enemies. You can't fight everyone. Keep the peace where you can, so you can focus where you must.
  • Remember they remember. Rivals recall how you've treated them, and it shapes how they'll treat you.
  • Alliances cut both ways. An ally brings help, and their wars.
  • Regard can be bought, and repaired. A timely gift or amends for an old grievance can head off a war, or open a treaty they'd otherwise refuse. Spend it where it changes something.
  • Pressure has a price. Demanding tribute or denouncing a rival works, but it's remembered. Use it against those you don't need as friends.
  • Wars can be shared. A friendly power will often join a war against your enemy, and a lukewarm one may for a price.
  • Your rivals play this game too. They court the strong, turn others against the leader, and squeeze the weak. A gift from a neighbour tells you they're afraid; a denunciation tells you you're the one to beat.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping expansion too early.
  • Having no clear goal, or never changing it when the game changes.
  • Noticing a rival's victory too late.
  • Attacking without enough strength, or without a way to finish the job.
  • Fighting with an outdated fleet.
  • Letting the treasury fall into debt.
  • Leaving the capital undefended.
  • Ignoring threats from outside until they're at your door.
  • Running the fuel reserve dry in the middle of a war.
  • Fighting a lost battle to the end instead of withdrawing.

Settings and music

You can shape each game on the new-game form: the galaxy's size, your rivals and how hard they play (with the computer players' options), standard or open play, pirates and creatures, the Wardens, new sectors, and corridor collapses. Choose a harder or longer game once you know how the pieces fit together.

Music. Dominion has a soundtrack. The main theme opens the game, and after that the music follows the state of the galaxy: exploring, at war, or facing the Wardens. Some tracks play for a long stretch before the next one. The ♪ button turns music on or off. Menu → Music has the volume, Next track, and Loop this track to keep one playing. Your choices are remembered on this device.
